articles.title: Castleton night works: Manchester Road’s three traffic phases
articles.excerpt: Overnight restrictions run until 8 November. The council has not published dates for individual phases.
articles.content_html:
Manchester Road drivers face overnight restrictions for Bee Network Phase 2 resurfacing, scheduled from 12 October to 8 November 2026, 8pm–5am. Only one phase operates at a time.

Phase 1 closes Manchester Road between Onslow Street and Bolton Road. Silk Street is westbound-only from Tesco to Manchester Road; right turns from Bolton Road onto Manchester Road are banned.

Phase 2 bans north-eastbound travel on Manchester Road from Bolton Road to Roch Valley Way. There is no left turn from Bolton Road onto Manchester Road. The old Manchester Road section must exit via Roch Valley Way. Manchester Road traffic can only turn left onto Bolton Road. Westbound travel on Silk Street from Tesco to Manchester Road is prohibited.

Phase 3 bans south-westbound travel between Roch Valley Way and Bolton Road. There is no left turn from Edinburgh Way onto Manchester Road, or right turn from Roch Valley Way. Silk Street closes between Manchester Road and Tesco, with no right turn into it from Manchester Road.

Diversions will be signed. Check the current phase before travelling: https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/directory-record/2618/various-roads-roadworks-in-rochdale-from-12-october-2026

articles.title: Does a boggart still haunt Clegg Hall?
articles.excerpt: Clegg Hall’s ghost story is a durable piece of local folklore; the house, its dates and ownership are documented, the murder-and-mooring tale is a later literary concoction with no contemporary record.
articles.summary: Clegg Hall’s ghost story is a durable piece of local folklore; the house, its dates and ownership are documented, the murder-and-mooring tale is a later literary concoction with no contemporary record.
articles.body:
Clegg Hall is a real place: a two‑storey stone house on Clegg Hall Road near Smithy Bridge, recorded in the National Heritage List for England as a Grade II* building (List Entry 1309615). The present house is dated to about 1610, appears in a 1626 manor survey as “a faire capital messuage” with gardens and fishponds, and its later ownership and sales are traceable in local estate records. Those facts are documentary and not in dispute (Historic England; History of the Parish of Rochdale). 

What gives the hall its fame is not the ledger but the story that a malevolent spirit — the “Clegg Hall boggart” — haunts the place after an uncle murdered his nephews and threw them into a moat. That version, vivid in print and oral tradition, comes to us through Victorian and later folklorists rather than contemporary chronicles. The most influential written account is John Roby’s 19th‑century chapter in Traditions of Lancashire, which retells ballads and local tellings and greatly embellishes the narrative. Roby’s tale and the ballads he used are literary sources for the boggart tradition, not legal or parish records. 

Historians who have examined the documentary record are clear about the difference. The county history that summarises parish records — drawing on deeds, surveys and earlier local historians — notes the same ghost tradition but says Roby’s story is “pure imagination” and finds no evidence to support the lurid murder tale. The same history traces land transfers of the Clegg, Belfield and neighbouring families across the 13th–17th centuries and records the sale of the “capital messuage called Clegg Hall” in 1618; it identifies the present building as probably erected in the early 17th century. In short: the house and its ownership are verifiable; the specific murder described in the legend is not supported by the surviving primary records (History of the Parish of Rochdale; Victoria County History material cited by Historic England). 

That does not mean the story appeared from nowhere. Folklore scholars and local chroniclers note that many Lancashire houses attract boggart‑type tales — often to explain an awkward inheritance, a ruined family line or strange noises at night — and such stories were widely collected and popularised in the 18th and 19th centuries. The county history records that a proverb, “As ill as Clegg Hall boggart,” was once current locally, showing the tale’s reach in speech even if its facts are unproven. 

What the written sources do confirm is more prosaic: fishponds and the hall’s setting are mentioned in early surveys; the surviving stone house is of Jacobean character and is legally protected as a listed building. Historic England’s listing (List Entry 1309615) gives the building’s architectural description and references the county history and earlier local historians as sources for the house’s documentary history. It does not record any verified crime or skeletal remains tied to the boggart legend. 

So what should a Rochdale reader take away? If you mean “Is there credible historical evidence that two children were murdered at Clegg Hall and that their deaths produced a haunting?” the answer is no: no contemporaneous court, parish or manorial record has been found that documents such a crime, and local historians treat the narrative as folkloric. If you mean “Is the boggart part of local culture?” absolutely: Roby, ballad fragments and the county history show a lively oral and printed tradition that became part of local speech. 

If you want to follow this up, start with the primary sources: the Historic England listing for the building (gives the architectural facts and listing number) and the county parish history, which summarises deeds and surveys and explicitly distinguishes the tradition from documentary evidence. For students of folklore, Roby’s Traditions of Lancashire is the principal 19th‑century source for the Clegg Hall boggart and for the ballads that shaped the modern story. 

The Clegg Hall boggart still lives: in books, local proverbs and on walking routes where people like a story to tell. It does not, on present evidence, live in chancery rolls or parish registers. In matters of tragedy and allegation, the surviving records — or the lack of them — remain the responsibly reported fact.

articles.title: Lifts at Freehold Tram Stop Out of Service Until Further Notice
articles.excerpt: The lifts at Freehold Tram Stop are currently out of service due to replacement works, affecting journeys towards Manchester and Rochdale.
articles.content_html:
The lifts at Freehold Tram Stop are out of service as of 6:59pm on Sunday, 18 October 2026, due to ongoing lift replacement works. This affects both platforms, with the lift towards Manchester and the lift towards Rochdale currently unavailable.

Passengers are advised to alight at either South Chadderton or Westwood tram stops and use the orange call point located at all stops to request assistance for completing their journeys. For further assistance, customers can contact the helpline at 0161 244 1000, which operates from 7am to 8pm on weekdays and 8am to 8pm on weekends and bank holidays.

The duration of the lift outage is currently unspecified, and no further updates have been provided regarding when the service will resume. Passengers are encouraged to plan their journeys accordingly and allow extra time for travel.

Transport for Greater Manchester apologises for any inconvenience caused by this disruption and is working to resolve the issue as quickly as possible.

articles.title: Secondary school applications close on 31 October: what Rochdale parents need to know
articles.excerpt: The council advises families to list five preferences and apply by Saturday 31 October. Late applications are considered after National Offer Day on 1 March 2027.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale families have until Saturday 31 October 2026 to apply for a secondary school place through the council's online parent portal.

With the deadline approaching, the council advises parents to name five school preferences. Repeating a school, or listing just one, does not improve the chance of securing it.

Applying on time matters. The council says 331 families applied late last year: 51% received their first preference, compared with 87% of applicants who met the deadline. Those figures describe last year's admissions, not a guarantee for this round.

Late applications are considered after National Offer Day, 1 March 2027. Schools do not hold places back for late applicants, so a preferred school may already be full.

Before submitting, read each school's admissions criteria, prospectus and Ofsted report. An on-time application still does not guarantee a preferred place.

Official deadline, guidance and admissions link: https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/news/article/675/council-urges-families-to-apply-on-time-for-secondary-school-places

articles.title: Crewe Alexandra Defeats Rochdale 3-2 in Record-Breaking Match
articles.excerpt: Crewe Alexandra secured a 3-2 victory over Rochdale, marking a record-breaking start to their league campaign. Manager Lee Bell praised his team's performance and resilience against a strong Rochdale side.
articles.content_html:
Crewe Alexandra achieved a significant milestone in their league campaign with a 3-2 victory over Rochdale on Saturday, October 17. This win marks Crewe's unbeaten streak of 11 games, setting a record for the club as they approach their 150th anniversary in 2027.

Manager Lee Bell expressed his pride in the team's performance, highlighting the importance of the victory. He stated, "It’s a big achievement with the club being 150 years old and for my players and staff to hold that record outright." Crewe's goals came from Matus Holicek and a brace from Jordan Gibson, who played a crucial role in the match despite a second-half fightback from Rochdale.

Rochdale, who had been on a five-game unbeaten run, struggled to contain Crewe's attacking play. Bell noted that while Rochdale played well, they did not pose a significant threat. He remarked, "When you’re 3-0 at home you do want it to be more comfortable than it was," referring to the pressure his team faced as Rochdale brought on their substitute Emmanuel Dieseruvwe.

The match saw Crewe take an early lead with Holicek's powerful strike followed by Gibson's two goals. Despite a late resurgence from Rochdale, including a goal from Joel Tabiner and a header from Aden Flint, Crewe held on to secure the win. This result not only boosts Crewe's confidence but also reinforces their position at the top of the league as they continue their impressive start to the season.

articles.title: Rochdale Unemployment Claimants Rise to 8,675 in August 2026
articles.excerpt: The number of people claiming unemployment-related benefits in Rochdale increased by 190 in August 2026, reflecting ongoing economic challenges in the area.
articles.content_html:
The number of people claiming unemployment-related benefits in Rochdale rose by 190 in August 2026, bringing the total to 8,675. This figure represents 6.0% of residents aged 16 to 64, an increase from 5.8% in July 2026.

In August 2025, the claimant count was slightly higher at 8,680, indicating a marginal decrease year-on-year. The latest figures were published by the Office for National Statistics through Nomis and are provisional, meaning they may be revised in future reports.

The rise in claimants reflects ongoing economic challenges faced by the local community, which may impact local businesses and services as more residents seek support. This increase highlights the need for further employment initiatives in the area.

Residents and local businesses may want to monitor these trends closely, as fluctuations in unemployment can affect economic stability and community resources.

articles.title: Rochdale’s £5m crisis support fund: what help is available this winter and how to ask
articles.excerpt: The council lists help with sudden financial emergencies, housing costs and essential goods. Different schemes have different rules; an award is not automatic.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale residents struggling to afford essentials can ask about support through the council's Crisis and Resilience Fund as winter approaches.

The £5 million programme runs from 1 April 2026 to 31 March 2027, using Department for Work and Pensions funding. It replaced the Household Support Fund in April. The £5 million is the borough-wide programme budget, not an amount available to each household.

The council lists several routes: Crisis Payments for sudden financial difficulty; Housing Payments for emergency rent or housing costs; the Discretionary Crisis Fund for goods; and Healthy Homes grants for eligible vulnerable residents needing help such as boiler repairs or essential appliances. Each route needs its own eligibility check.

For Crisis Payments, eligible residents can receive a voucher worth up to £75 towards food and energy. Applicants must live in Rochdale borough, be at least 16 and have nobody receiving Child Benefit for them. Applications are allowed once every six months. Apply by calling 01706 923685; the published hours are Monday to Friday, 9am–5pm. Examples of a crisis include fire, flooding, a health emergency or losing employment.

The separate Discretionary Crisis Fund is described as last-resort support. It provides goods rather than cash. Its contact number is 01706 532222 and its email is StrategicHousing@rochdale.gov.uk.

Check the route that matches your circumstances before applying. The main fund page also mentions food vouchers only through the end of the 2026 summer holidays; that wording does not establish a winter voucher entitlement.

articles.title: Rochdale Sleep Out Raises Funds for Homeless Support
articles.excerpt: Fundraisers gathered at Crown Oil Arena for the annual Sleep Out, raising awareness and funds for homelessness initiatives in the community.
articles.content_html:
Fundraisers spent a night outdoors at Rochdale's Crown Oil Arena to raise awareness and vital funds for people experiencing homelessness. This event, the second annual Sleep Out organised by Petrus Communities and RAFC Community Trust, saw supporters from across the borough come together for a common cause.

The money raised will support the Changing Lives initiative, a football programme designed to assist individuals facing homelessness or living in supported accommodation. The initiative aims to enhance participants' mental health, physical well-being, and social inclusion through free football sessions, while also providing personal development opportunities, including pathways into volunteering, education, and employment.

Louise Scriven, Fundraising and Partnerships Coordinator at Petrus, emphasised that the Sleep Out is not about pretending to experience homelessness, but about standing in solidarity with those facing housing insecurities. She noted that last year's event significantly impacted participants, helping them rebuild confidence, forge new friendships, and develop skills to become active community members.

The funds raised from this year's Sleep Out will continue to provide essential accommodation, support, advice, and opportunities for those experiencing homelessness and disadvantage in Rochdale, Oldham, and Burnley. Donations are crucial for sustaining these services and making a difference in the lives of vulnerable individuals in the community.

articles.title: Rochdale Council Rejects Car Wash Proposal at Former Paul Price Cars Site
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Council's planning committee has refused a proposal to establish a car wash at the former Paul Price Cars site on Kingsway, despite initial recommendations for approval.
articles.content_html:
A proposal to demolish the former Paul Price Cars building at 311 Kingsway, Rochdale, and replace it with a car wash has been refused by Rochdale Council's planning committee. The application, submitted by Matthew Gray, aimed to create five jet-wash bays along with a laundrette pod, a dog wash pod, and a vending machine.

Despite planning officers recommending approval, the committee ultimately decided against the plans. Supporting documents for the application argued that the development would enhance the area, which is currently considered a blight due to the building's appearance. The documents stated that the proposal would provide a beneficial facility and would have a lower visual impact compared to the existing structure when viewed from the Rochdale Bypass.

The application was described as a small-scale development that would complement the existing uses in the area, referencing previous approvals for car wash facilities at the site. However, the committee's refusal indicates that concerns about the proposal outweighed the perceived benefits.

As it stands, the future of the site remains uncertain. Matthew Gray has not yet indicated whether he will appeal the decision or submit a revised application. Local residents and businesses will be keen to see what happens next, as the site continues to be a point of contention in the community.

articles.title: Rochdale man refused permission to appeal Manchester Airport assault sentence
articles.excerpt: Mohammed Fahir Amaaz, from Rochdale, has been refused permission to appeal against his 42-month sentence following assaults at Manchester Airport, according to sources.
articles.content_html:
A Rochdale man jailed after assaulting two police officers and a member of the public at Manchester Airport has been refused permission to appeal against his sentence, according to sources.

Mohammed Fahir Amaaz, 21, was sentenced at Liverpool Crown Court on 26 June 2026 to 42 months in prison. The Crown Prosecution Service confirmed his convictions were for assault occasioning actual bodily harm, assault by beating and assault on an emergency worker.

His renewed application for permission to appeal against sentence was scheduled before the Court of Appeal in London on Friday 16 October. The published court listing placed the case in Court 6 at 10am, under reference 202602577.

Before the hearing, his solicitors, Imran Khan and Partners, said a single judge had refused his initial application on 14 August. His legal team then renewed the application to the full court. Friday’s proceedings concerned permission to challenge his sentence.

The convictions arose from events at Manchester Airport on 23 July 2024. According to the CPS, the incident began when Amaaz assaulted a passenger inside the Terminal 2 Starbucks and continued in another part of the airport when police arrived to arrest him. One officer suffered a broken nose.

The offences for which he was sentenced involved member of the public Abdulkareem Hamzah Abbas Ismaeil, PC Lydia Ward and PC Ellie Cook.

A separate allegation involving PC Zachary Marsden must be distinguished from those convictions. Amaaz and his brother, Muhammad Amaad, also from Rochdale, faced that allegation, but two juries were unable to reach verdicts. In May 2026, the prosecution offered no further evidence and not guilty verdicts were recorded.

The sentence application listed on Friday was in Mohammed Fahir Amaaz’s name. Rochdale Daily will update this report if the court’s detailed reasons or a further statement from his legal representatives become available.

articles.title: St Cuthbert’s evacuated as message reassures parents all children and staff are safe
articles.excerpt: St Teresa of Calcutta Catholic Academy Trust says St Cuthbert’s was evacuated following a possible bomb threat. All children and staff are safe; parents can collect pupils.
articles.content_html:
Latest update — St Teresa of Calcutta trust statement

St Teresa of Calcutta Catholic Academy Trust, which oversees St Cuthbert’s RC High School, has released a statement saying staff received a communication detailing a possible bomb threat on Friday morning, 16 October.

The trust says emergency services were called, all school buildings were evacuated as a precaution and Greater Manchester Police attended. All children and staff are safe and accounted for, it says.

Parents and carers can now collect their children or give consent for them to travel home, according to the statement. The trust says specialist security operatives will carry out a full sweep of the building this afternoon. It currently expects the school to reopen as normal on Monday 19 October, subject to further updates.

The trust’s account conflicts with some earlier reports circulating about the incident. In particular, it describes rumours of intruders or weapons on school premises as false. Earlier references to a lockdown should be read alongside this latest statement, which describes a precautionary evacuation following a possible bomb threat.

This remains a developing story. Rochdale Daily will continue to update this article with official information as it is released. The earlier updates below are retained for context; the latest trust statement takes precedence where accounts differ.

Trust statement in full:

Earlier this morning (Friday 16 October 2026), staff at St. Cuthbert's RC High School in Rochdale received a communication detailing a possible bomb threat to the premises.

The emergency services were called and all school buildings were evacuated as a precautionary measure.

All children and staff are safe and accounted for, in line with our established procedures.

Greater Manchester Police attended and parents and carers were notified immediately that their children had been removed to a safe distance and there was no threat or danger to anyone present.

We would like to assure everyone within the St Cuthbert’s School community that the safety and wellbeing of our children remains our absolute priority.

Specialist security operatives will conduct a full sweep of the building this afternoon to confirm if any further actions are required.

Currently, the expectation is that the school will be open as normal on Monday 19 October - but further information will be communicated as needed when received.

Parents and carers can now attend the school to collect their children, or provide consent for their children to travel home.

We’d like to thank parents, carers and colleagues for their understanding and co-operation in this matter.

We’d also urge people to avoid speculation on social media - particularly regarding false rumours, such as any referring to intruders or weapons being present on school premises.

More details will be communicated when appropriate, following consultation with GMP and Rochdale Borough Council.

Source: Statement attributed to St Teresa of Calcutta Catholic Academy Trust, supplied to Rochdale Daily on 16 October 2026.

Earlier updates — before the trust statement

Developing update — councillor requests official briefing

Councillor Jordan Tarrant-Short has said he is urgently requesting an update from Rochdale Council and Greater Manchester Police following reports of a lockdown at Saint Cuthbert’s High School. In a statement supplied to Rochdale Daily, he said he first learned of the reports through the Manchester Evening News and had not received an official briefing.

His statement does not establish what prompted the incident. The earlier message shared with Rochdale Daily described a precautionary evacuation and said all children and staff were safe and accounted for.

Councillor Tarrant-Short’s statement in full:

I want to address the reports of a lockdown at Saint Cuthbert’s High School.

First and foremost, my thoughts are with the children, their families and the staff. I understand how frightening this situation will be, particularly for parents waiting for information and reassurance.

I want to be clear: I first became aware of this through the Manchester Evening News. I have not received an official briefing.

I am now urgently requesting an update from Rochdale Council and Greater Manchester Police so I can understand what has happened and what support is being provided to those affected.

Having been through a similar situation myself when Newhouse Academy went into lockdown, I know how distressing that uncertainty can feel. Behind every update are children who may be frightened and families desperate to know their loved ones are safe.

I am asking that communication with families is timely, clear and compassionate, and that support is available for anyone left distressed.

Until there is verified information, I will not speculate about the circumstances. Please follow official updates from the school and police, and avoid sharing rumours.

The immediate priority must be the safety and wellbeing of every child and member of staff.

articles.excerpt: Following a High Court ruling, Rochdale Council has confirmed plans to redevelop Hopwood Hall, with an emphasis on community use, after ending an exclusivity agreement with Hopwood DePree.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Council has announced its commitment to the redevelopment of Hopwood Hall following a recent High Court ruling that upheld the council's decision to terminate an exclusivity agreement with American filmmaker Hopwood DePree. The ruling, delivered at Manchester Civil Justice Centre, concluded that the council acted lawfully when it ended the agreement, which had been in place since 2017.

The council leader, Neil Emmott, addressed the future of the historic building during a town hall meeting on October 15, stating that the council is focused on bringing Hopwood Hall back into use for the community. Emmott expressed openness to DePree's involvement, indicating that if he presents a viable plan, the council would consider it. However, he noted that the legal process is not yet concluded, as DePree has the option to appeal the decision by November 18, 2026, with a potential extension to November 28, 2026.

The High Court's decision came after DePree claimed he had a legally binding agreement to purchase the hall for £1, based on a planning approval granted in 2022. However, the court found that this approval did not trigger the option to purchase. The council has already invested over £1.6 million in repairs to the hall, and Emmott assured that any costs awarded to the council, amounting to £114,000, would be reinvested into the project.

As the situation develops, the council remains committed to the restoration and preservation of Hopwood Hall, which is seen as a valuable asset for the local community. Emmott reiterated that the council's focus is on securing the hall's long-term future, and the outcome of any potential appeal will be crucial in determining the next steps.

articles.title: Rochdale Council Addresses Concerns Over Local Pub Closures
articles.excerpt: Councillor Richard Jackson has raised concerns about the future of local pubs in Littleborough after the closure of The Wheatsheaf, highlighting restrictive covenants that hinder reopening efforts.
articles.content_html:
The future of local pubs in Littleborough is under scrutiny following the recent closure of The Wheatsheaf. This closure has sparked community outcry and raised concerns about the viability of pubs in the area. Councillor Richard Jackson addressed these issues during a Rochdale council meeting on October 15, highlighting the challenges posed by restrictive covenants that prevent former pubs from being reopened as such.

Councillor Jackson noted that approximately 50 per cent of pubs are owned by breweries or large pub companies, which often include covenants in sales to deter competition. This practice has led to a significant number of closures, with many pubs being sold off for alternative uses. He cited the example of the former Royal Oak pub, which closed in 2015 and was subsequently converted into a vape shop, a change that was later halted by Trading Standards due to regulatory issues.

The council's discussion aims to address the ongoing loss of pubs in the community, with Jackson's motion seeking to reduce the impact of these covenants. He expressed concern over the cycle of tenant attrition that many pubs face, stating, "We have seen this at the former Royal Oak pub. This was sold with an anti-competition covenant."

The implications of this discussion are significant for local residents and pub enthusiasts, as the council considers measures to protect these community assets. The outcome of this motion could influence future policies regarding the sale and repurposing of pubs in Littleborough and beyond.

Is the future of the local pub in danger? That’s the fear in Littleborough where the closure of another pub has sparked outcry. A few months ago The Wheatsheaf closed down in the Rochdalian town. There is strong community interest in reopening the pub as a local asset, but a small loophole means they fear they can’t do that. When breweries or large companies that own and operate pubs sell on the building, they can include a covenant that prevents it from being re-used as a pub. This covenant is inserted into a sale to stop competitors taking the pub on the cheap, the latest town hall meeting was told. Coun Richard Jackson brought forward a motion to Rochdale council to address this very issue to reduce the continued loss of pubs in communities. The Littleborough Lakeside councillor told the chamber on October 15: “The reality is that around 50 per cent of pubs are owned by breweries or large pub companies. They have a history of damaging the industry as a whole. This often leads to tenant attrition. “We are acutely aware of pubs being closed down after numerous tenants have left the building. The point of this motion is to address the churn. “We have seen this at the former Royal Oak pub. This was sold with an anti-competition covenant.” The former Royal Oak pub was closed down in 2015 and then sold off and became a vape shop, which was later shut down by Trading Standards. Coun Jackson called on the council to write to the government to block restrictive covenants on pub sales. He said that this loophole means most pubs get turned into shops or HMOs. His ward colleague Coun Tom Besford shared his annoyance that the future use of a community building can be dictated by the business interests of a brewery or company. The pair also credited Rochdale MP Paul Waugh for his continued work on this issue and raising it in Parliament. Speaking after the motion was passed in Rochdale Town Hall, Mr Waugh said: “This Government has already done the heavy lifting on pubs. Since August, the planning rules make it harder to turn a viable pub into flats or a shop, and the new Community Right to Buy gives people the power to buy their local. articles.title: Young people inspire £85,000–£100,000 Castleton pump track proposal
articles.excerpt: A site beside the yellow play park on Manchester Road is being explored for a Castleton bike track, with young people helping shape the idea. Funding and approvals remain outstanding.
articles.content_html:
A new pump track costing an estimated £85,000 to £100,000 is being explored for Castleton after local young people asked for somewhere closer to home to ride their bikes.

Councillor Dave Jones said an area beside the yellow play park on Manchester Road had emerged as a promising potential location following discussions with council officers and youth workers.

The proposal remains at an early stage. No funding or final site approval has been announced, and there is no confirmed construction timetable.

In an update shared with Rochdale Daily, Cllr Jones described a positive meeting with Environmental Management, township officer Caroline and Jasmin from the Youth Work Team to discuss the concept.

Several possible locations were considered. According to the councillor, young people suggested the Manchester Road site because it feels safe. Its existing play area and car park could also make it convenient for families with children of different ages.

The idea is for younger children to use the playground while older children and teenagers could enjoy a nearby bike track, bringing different activities together in one central location.

Cllr Jones said those at the meeting supported involving young people in the design process. They also discussed whether contractors could explain how the track is built and explore suitable opportunities for young people to participate.

A bike repair hub was another suggestion. Local young people have spoken about their interest in repairing bicycles and sharing those skills with others. Secure bike storage lockers were also raised during the discussions.

The councillor said some young people currently travel to tracks elsewhere in the borough, including Littleborough, and expressed concern about the busy roads those journeys can involve. He believes a Castleton facility could offer a more convenient option and reassurance for families.

Funding is the main obstacle. Cllr Jones put the initial estimated cost at between £85,000 and £100,000 and said several processes and approvals would need to be completed before any scheme could proceed.

Council officers are now exploring possible funding sources, according to his update. A further meeting is planned to discuss potential designs and ensure any future proposal reflects what local young people want.

Cllr Jones also thanked Keane, the young person who first approached him with the idea, and praised young residents for taking an active role in improving their community.

He cautioned: “It's important to stress that projects like this take time, and there is still a long way to go.”

The potential location, repair hub, storage lockers and construction involvement are all ideas under discussion rather than confirmed features of an approved scheme.

articles.title: St Cuthbert’s RC High School Closes Following Bomb Threat
articles.excerpt: St Cuthbert’s RC High School in Rochdale was evacuated and closed on 16 October after receiving a suspected bomb threat. All students and staff were reported safe, and police are investigating the incident.
articles.content_html:
St Cuthbert’s RC High School in Rochdale was evacuated and closed on Friday morning, 16 October, after staff received a communication regarding a possible bomb threat. The school, located on Shaw Road, implemented emergency procedures to ensure the safety of all students and staff.

In response to the threat, Greater Manchester Police were called to the scene, and the school entered a lockdown as a precautionary measure. A spokesperson for the school confirmed that all children and staff were safe and accounted for during the incident. The police assessed the situation and indicated that the call was likely a hoax.

The St Teresa of Calcutta Catholic Academy Trust, which oversees the school, stated that specialist security operatives would conduct a thorough sweep of the premises to determine if any further action was necessary. Parents and carers were informed that they could collect their children or give permission for them to travel home safely.

The school is expected to reopen as normal on Monday, 19 October, pending the outcome of the police investigation. Authorities have urged the public to refrain from speculation on social media regarding false rumours related to the incident.

articles.title: Rochdale Fitness Group to Undertake 100km Arctic Challenge for Cancer Charities
articles.excerpt: Eighteen runners from Resilience gym in Rochdale will embark on a 100km run across the Arctic wilderness on January 29, 2027, to raise funds for cancer charities.
articles.content_html:
A local fitness community in Rochdale is gearing up for a challenging 100-kilometre run across the Arctic wilderness of Swedish Lapland, set to take place on January 29, 2027. The event, known as the Ultra 4 Cancer challenge, will see 18 runners from Resilience gym tackle extreme conditions, including temperatures that may plunge to -30°C, over the course of two days.

The initiative is led by Martin Stapleton, founder and head coach of Resilience gym. Stapleton, a Rochdale-born former Royal Marines Commando and professional MMA fighter, has a history of extreme fundraising efforts, including kayaking the length of the Rochdale Canal and running along the River Thames to support Help for Heroes. Joining him on this expedition are assistant coaches Greg Egan and Oliver Roxburgh, the latter of whom has a personal connection to the cause.

The team aims to raise vital funds for four cancer charities, highlighting the importance of community support in tackling such a significant health issue. The challenge not only tests the physical endurance of the participants but also serves to raise awareness and funds for cancer research and support services.

As the date approaches, the runners will be preparing for the harsh conditions they will face, with training sessions likely to intensify. Community members interested in supporting the cause can follow the team's progress and contribute to their fundraising efforts through the Resilience gym's social media channels.

Terms and conditions Read the terms and conditions of using the data and images. About the data The data provides the food hygiene rating or inspection result given to a business and reflect the standards of food hygiene found on the date of inspection or visit by the local authority. Businesses include restaurants, pubs, cafés, takeaways, hotels and other places consumers eat, as well as supermarkets and other food shops. The data are held on behalf of local authorities participating in either the: national Food Hygiene Rating Scheme (FHRS) in England, Northern Ireland and Wales, or the Food Hygiene Information Scheme (FHIS) in Scotland Data for local authority areas running either of these schemes can be found on the Ratings site: See a list of local authorities running the FHRS or FHIS The scores part of the data is only applicable to scheme type FHRS (not FHIS) and are for hygiene, structure and confidence in management. These scores can be found in part 2 and 3 of Annex 1, A1.1 of the Food Law code of Practice . These scores are then used to calculate the food hygiene rating details of which can be found in the Guidance on implementation and operation of the Food Hygiene Rating Scheme: the Brand Standard and statutory guidance . articles.title: Rochdale Council Celebrates Achievements of Over 200 Cared-for Children at Annual Awards
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Council hosted its annual awards ceremony at Matthew Moss High School, recognising the achievements of more than 200 cared-for children with medals and a day of entertainment.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Council held its annual awards ceremony on 16 October at Matthew Moss High School, celebrating the achievements of over 200 cared-for children. The event, known as 'Our Big Day', recognised the resilience and determination of young people in care, with hundreds of medals awarded to honour their individual successes.

The council received 273 nominations from carers, teachers, and social workers, highlighting the inspiring journeys of children up to the age of 12. Awards were given for exceptional progress in education, sporting achievements, acts of kindness, and positive attitudes in the face of adversity. The day included a variety of entertainment, such as trampolines, funfair rides, and face painting, allowing families to create joyful memories together.

Councillor Rachel Massey, cabinet member for children’s services and education, expressed her pride in the achievements of the children, stating, "They are all exceptional young people and show phenomenal determination to be their very best. This doesn’t go unnoticed by those around them." The event aimed to provide public recognition for the hard work and accomplishments of these young individuals.

Local businesses sponsored the celebration, contributing to the activities and entertainment provided for families. Notable sponsors included A&T Surfacing Ltd, Rochdale Boroughwide Housing, and Rochdale Hornets, among others. This community support helped create a memorable day for the children and their families.

articles.title: The Healey Dell prophecy: the Lady Eleanor who was said to be 'maid, wife and widow in one day'
articles.excerpt: A short guide to the strange Healey Dell story about Eleanor Byron and a fortune‑teller called Mother Bagden — what the old printed collectors actually recorded, what local guides now tell visitors, and what survives as verifiable fact.
articles.summary: A short guide to the strange Healey Dell story about Eleanor Byron and a fortune‑teller called Mother Bagden — what the old printed collectors actually recorded, what local guides now tell visitors, and what survives as verifiable fact.
articles.body:
Healey Dell’s cleft in the Spodden — the narrow gorge known locally as the Thrutch and the spot tourists call the Fairies’ Chapel — is one of Rochdale borough’s most durable story‑places. The best‑known version of the tale says a local noblewoman, usually called Lady Eleanor (linked by later tellings to the Byron family), visited a fortune‑teller named Mother Bagden; the woman prophesied Eleanor would be a maid, a wife and a widow all in one day, and on her wedding day the bridegroom was killed. That dramatic sequence is recorded in early nineteenth‑century folklore collectors and is the version repeated by the Dell’s modern heritage interpretation. ([gutenberg.org](https://www.gutenberg.org/files/25256/25256-h/25256-h.htm))

The oldest printed witness we can point to is John Roby’s Traditions of Lancashire, collected and published in the early 1800s; Roby preserves a long, romance‑style narrative set at Healey that includes a miller, a Fairy‑Chapel, a talisman and the fatal wedding night that fulfils the prophecy. Roby’s book is literary folklore: it records what people were telling in his day rather than supplying contemporary medieval documents about the events described. ([gutenberg.org](https://www.gutenberg.org/files/25256/25256-h/25256-h.htm))

Local interpretation and visitor material at Healey Dell — the Heritage Centre and the site’s guides — now knit Roby’s account together with later Victorian retellings (and with local names such as Chadwick and Healey Hall). The Heritage Centre openly treats the story as legend and presents it alongside geology, mill remains and an account of the great flood of 4 July 1838 that altered the Thrutch feature generations later. Those local guides also cite later local antiquarians (for example William Robertson’s regional histories) as sources for the familiar version. In short: the prophecy story is part of the Dell’s storytelling tradition, preserved in printed collections and in modern visitor interpretation, not in contemporary court rolls or parish registers. ([healeydelltearooms.co.uk](https://www.healeydelltearooms.co.uk/things-to-do/the-fairies-chapel/))

What is documentary fact here, and what is folklore? Verifiable facts: Healey Dell exists as a managed nature reserve and visitor attraction at 121 Dell Road; the valley contains recognisable industrial archaeology (old mill sites, lodges and a prominent Victorian railway viaduct) and a heritage centre with displays and family trails. Rochdale Borough Council provides the site address, facilities and opening information; the viaduct itself is a Grade II listed structure on the National Heritage List for England. Those are public, documentable features you can still see. ([rochdale.gov.uk](https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/directory-record/737/healey-dell-nature-reserve-and-tea-rooms-rochdale))

What cannot be verified in the surviving records is the supernatural machinery of the tale: a Fairy Queen who issued prophecies, a coven turned to stone, or a named medieval Lady Eleanor whose wedding‑night fate is confirmed in a contemporary legal or parish document. The earliest printed accounts that give the prophecy its shape are collectors’ and antiquarian narratives from the nineteenth century; later guidebooks and the Heritage Centre responsibly present them as legend rather than as archival history. If a claim about a medieval event cannot be found in contemporary documents, it belongs to folklore and local tradition rather than to proven local history. ([gutenberg.org](https://www.gutenberg.org/files/25256/25256-h/25256-h.htm))

For readers who want to follow the trace: read Roby’s Traditions of Lancashire for the early printed tale; visit the Healey Dell Heritage Centre for the site interpretation and the leaflet material that draws the story together; and see the viaduct and river features for the physical reasons people long ago imagined a tiny ‘chapel’ there. The council’s directory entry gives practical details (address, parking, facilities and the fact the park area is open daily). The short, final point is this: the prophecy of Mother Bagden and Lady Eleanor is an old and well‑preserved piece of Lancashire storytelling — entertaining and locally meaningful — but it should be read as folklore, not as a documented historical event.

articles.title: Nine-Year-Old Guitar Virtuoso Adrian Abraham from Middleton on Verge of World Record
articles.excerpt: Adrian Abraham, a nine-year-old from Middleton, is set to make his mark in the music world as he approaches a potential world record for his guitar skills, inspired by his father and a passion for heavy metal.
articles.content_html:
Adrian Abraham, a nine-year-old guitar virtuoso from Middleton, is on the verge of setting a world record for his exceptional guitar skills. Having started his musical journey approximately two years ago, Adrian has rapidly developed his talent, showcasing his abilities through performances shared on his Instagram account.

Initially picking up an acoustic guitar, Adrian soon transitioned to electric guitar, where he found his passion for heavy metal music. Inspired by his father, who introduced him to the instrument, Adrian has dedicated himself to mastering various genres, although heavy metal remains his favourite.

As he prepares for his first live performance, Adrian aims to inspire others to take up an instrument, demonstrating that dedication and passion can lead to remarkable achievements at a young age. His journey reflects not only his personal growth but also the potential for young musicians to make an impact in the music industry.

Adrian's story is a testament to the power of inspiration and hard work, and as he approaches this potential world record, the local community is eager to support his musical aspirations.

Adrian Abraham, from Middleton, only started playing the guitar about two years ago. Later this month, he is taking the Trinity College London Grade 8 Rock & Pop electric guitar examination — and could win a Guinness World Record in the process. Adrian loves heavy metal and picked up the guitar after hearing his father, Abraham Joseph, play the acoustic guitar. His favourite band is Iron Maiden and his favourite song to play is Eruption, by Van Halen. His Instagram page features dozens of videos chronicling his journey, including performances of hits by Metallica, Guns ‘n’ Roses, Queen, Deep Purple, Slipknot and System of a Down. The youngster said: “I saw my dad playing the guitar and I thought it really sounded cool, and then I wanted to give it a try. Adrian prepares for his first live performance. Image: adrian_jaams “So then I gave it a shot and I started going through acoustic at first and eventually went to electric.” Abraham added: “I used to play acoustic guitar and he used to sit down and listen. One day he told me he wanted to just hold the guitar to get the feel of it. “He took the guitar and he held a perfect cord. That’s the time I realised the guitar is the instrument for him. “His first guitar was a classic acoustic guitar which he played for about three months before it wasn’t enough for him and we had to upgrade to an electric. He is really progressing well. “I’ve been in choirs and I picked up the acoustic guitar when I was in college. It was just for fun and then I left it, but then when Adrian was born, I had this overwhelming feeling I should play something to him which would sound good. Music brings the out a real person. “But then he reached a point where he discovering grade eight. I can only teach him as much as basics of the guitar but the further grades, he picked it up himself.” With the help of a tutor, Adrian could now become the youngest person to pass the Grade 8 rock and pop guitar exam, setting a world record. articles.title: Broadfield Park Slopes Renovation Celebrated at Rochdale Town Hall
articles.excerpt: A special event at Rochdale Town Hall recognised the contributions of volunteers and partners involved in the restoration of Broadfield Park Slopes, highlighting the project's community impact and heritage significance.
articles.content_html:
A celebration was held at Rochdale Town Hall to honour the individuals and groups who contributed to the renovation of Broadfield Park Slopes. This historic site, located between Rochdale Town Hall and St Chad’s Church, has undergone significant restoration, thanks to the efforts of local volunteers and funding from The National Lottery Heritage Fund.

The event, organised by Polly Brant, Cultural Engagement Officer for Rochdale Council, brought together volunteers, partners, and community members to acknowledge their roles in the project. Guests were treated to a series of films by local filmmaker Jack Grindrod, showcasing the stories and heritage associated with the park's transformation. The films captured the community involvement that played a crucial role in the renovation process.

The evening featured poetry readings by Alende Amisi, a local poet and former young poet in residence, who shared his personal reflections on Rochdale's heritage. His contributions added a personal touch to the event, which celebrated not only the park's restoration but also the community spirit that drove the project forward.

The renovation has restored the historic Packer Spout Fountain, created a new accessible pathway, improved landscaping, and introduced new heritage interpretation. The lower lawn has been terraced to create a natural amphitheatre, providing a new space for activities and events, enhancing the park's role as a community hub.

It has included 28 work placement students, 12 archaeological volunteers and a two year schools programme involving 715 pupils. articles.title: Rochdale Council Plans Major Investments and Heritage Restoration
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Council has announced significant investments in heritage restoration and community services, including plans for Hopwood Hall and Middleton's regeneration projects, aimed at boosting local economy and services.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Council has outlined a series of major investments aimed at revitalising the borough, with a focus on heritage restoration and community services. In a recent column, Councillor Neil Emmott highlighted the council's commitment to enhancing local infrastructure and supporting residents amid ongoing cost-of-living challenges.

A key development is the council's recent victory in the High Court regarding Hopwood Hall, a historic building in Middleton. The ruling provides clarity on the future of the site, which has seen over £1.6 million invested since 2017 by the council and Historic England. Plans for essential repairs and feasibility studies are underway, with the aim of restoring the hall to serve the community and preserve its historical significance.

In addition to Hopwood Hall, the council is advancing its regeneration plans for Middleton. The acquisition of Middleton Old Grammar School is expected to attract a new tenant by the end of the year, while the long-derelict Warwick Mill is also set for redevelopment, potentially including new housing. Furthermore, the transformation of the Middleton Scout Hut into a community venue is in progress, aimed at providing activities and training for young people.

These initiatives are part of a broader strategy to stimulate economic growth and create jobs across the borough. With banking and post office services returning to Middleton town centre in the new year, local leaders are optimistic about the positive impact these developments will have on the community.

articles.title: Jolly Josh welcomes Rochdale families with inclusive play, music and activity sessions
articles.excerpt: The Castleton charity is reaching out to families caring for children and young people with complex medical needs and physical disabilities, with weekly sessions and bookable activities.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale charity Jolly Josh is reaching out to families caring for children and young people with complex medical needs and physical disabilities, with a programme of inclusive activities and support.

Based at 2 Ensor Mill in Castleton, Rochdale, OL11 2NU, the centre welcomes children and young adults aged from birth to 19.

The charity says finding activities where a child is welcomed, understood and supported can be difficult, and wants more parents, carers, relatives and professionals to know what is available.

Its programme includes music and signing, themed play sessions, an after-school club, a youth group and activities that families can book directly with the centre.

Weekly sessions

Sing And Sign runs every Wednesday from 10.30am to 12.30pm, bringing together music, songs and signing to make communication fun.

Themed Stay And Play takes place every Tuesday and Saturday from 9.30am to 12.30pm. Sessions offer activities, friendship and a different theme each week.

Sensory Touch And Music runs every Thursday from 10am to noon, offering a relaxing sensory session.

The After School Club takes place every Wednesday from 4pm to 7pm, with inclusive activities and a light tea offered for every child.

The Youth Group meets every Thursday from 5pm to 8pm, giving young people a welcoming space to socialise, take part in activities and build friendships.

Activities available to book

Hydrotherapy sessions can be booked for families or with the centre’s Hydro Lead.

Private sound bath sessions are also available by contacting the centre, offering an opportunity to take time out of a busy schedule.

Rebound Therapy provides supported movement and sensory experiences using a trampoline, with sessions bookable through the centre.

How to get in touch

Parents, carers, family members and professionals supporting a child with complex medical needs are invited to contact Jolly Josh to learn more about its sessions.

Call 01706 399141, email sarah@jollyjosh.co.uk or visit https://jollyjosh.co.uk/

The centre asks anyone planning to visit to contact the team first so an appointment can be arranged.

Families can contact the centre to discuss which sessions suit their child and ask about booking, availability and charges.

The charity is also encouraging people to share its appeal with families who may not yet know about the support available.

evidence_sources.captured_text: Court rules in ownership row over Hopwood Hall - Rochdale Times Skip to content LATEST NEWS Court rules in ownership row over Hopwood Hall A court has ruled that Rochdale Council did not act unfairly in its decision not to pass ownership of Hopwood Hall to one of its descendants. Today marked the end of a two-day trial in the High Court in Manchester after Hopwood DePree took legal action against the council which ended an exclusivity agreement to sell the historic Grade II-listed hall to him. Following the decision, Mr DePree said: “This is of course incredibly disappointing and a huge blow to our community, our supporters around the world, as well as the UK’s charitable heritage rescue groups in general. “However, please know that my team and I are already determining our legal options and next steps. “We will be watching closely to keep an eye on Rochdale Borough Council’s efforts to save Hopwood Hall for the community, and restore it to its former glory.” Mr DePree is a descendant of the Hopwood family which build the manor house in the 1420s. The family owned the hall and surrounding land — which is now Hopwood Hall College — until 1922. The house was sold 20 years later. It was occupied by a variety of temporary residents, including the de la Salle Brothers, who ran it as a Catholic teacher training college until the 1980s. It had fallen into disrepair and was bought by Rochdale Council, which still owns the Grade II-listed property. READ MORE:Rochdale Diversity Awards 2026 Finalists Announced Mr DePree launched legal action after he spent seven years working with the council to carry out vital repairs on the dilapidated site with a view to purchasing it. In November, 2024, the council ended its exclusivity agreement with Mr DePree, and said it would explore other options because no “commercially viable” business model had been presented. Mr DePree and volunteers who worked on the hall have been barred from returning to the site since then. In the meantime, the council has spent £640,000 making the roof watertight. A council spokesperson said: “We are pleased with today’s judgement. It’s a shame that we had to endure a costly court battle to get to this point, as the time and money invested into this process could have been better spent on the hall itself. “We’re now focussed on moving forward. More than £1.6 million has been spent on the hall by ourselves and Historic England since 2017 and we will continue to invest in vital repairs to this historic building. “Feasibility studies have already been completed and options for Hopwood Hall’s long-term future will be considered in due course. “Whatever the future holds for Hopwood Hall, this building, once restored and refurbished, will be used for the benefit of the wider community of Middleton who rightly cherish it as an important part of Middleton’s rich and varied heritage.” SUPPORT THE ROCHDALE TIMES: FOLLOW US ON FACEBOOK Got a story?
